section_titles: Framing a question and collecting data
periods.activity_title: Which question works best for a survey?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Look at the questions asked by Rohan and Anjali, p.203
tasks_in_class.description: Tick the question that is the most appropriate for finding the 'most liked subject'. Why do you think so? Discuss with your friends and teacher.

time_bands.activity: Open the class with a quick show of hands: ask students to call out their favourite school subject freely. Record whatever they say on the board — some will name two subjects, some will give vague answers. Let the messiness sit visibly so students feel the problem of comparing unlike answers.

Direct students to Look at the questions asked by Rohan and Anjali, p.203 ("Tick the question most appropriate for finding the 'most liked subject'...."). In pairs, students read both question wordings and tick their choice. Each pair then explains aloud: what kind of answer would Rohan's open question produce? what kind would Anjali's produce? Why does one make counting easier?

Bring pairs together. Build a class consensus on the board: list the different types of answers each question would generate. Establish the principle — a survey question that asks for exactly one choice yields comparable, countable responses. Students record the agreed reason in their own words in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often assume any question works for a survey; the discussion should surface that open-ended questions produce answers that cannot be fairly counted against one another. Watch for students who say 'both questions are fine' — ask them to show how they would count the responses from Rohan's question fairly.

section_titles: Organising data into a frequency table
periods.activity_title: From messy list to tidy table

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Look at the children's responses above and answer the following questions, p.204
tasks_in_class.description: Fill in: the number of children who like Mathematics / Language / The World Around Us / Physical Education / Arts the most.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Now look at the above table and answer the following questions, p.205
tasks_in_class.description: Identify the most common and least common favourite subject. Then decide which of the two ways of displaying information (raw list vs. table) is easier to understand and why.

homework.book_ref: Let's fill the above information in this table, p.205
homework.description: Fill in the frequency table: Subjects (M, L, T, P.E., A) against number of children who like each subject the most.

time_bands.activity: Students open their textbooks to the raw list of 45 responses on p.204. Working individually, they tally each abbreviation (M, L, T, A, P.E.) using stroke marks on a rough count strip. Teacher circulates, asking: 'How are you keeping track so you do not count the same response twice?'

Students complete Look at the children's responses above and answer the following questions, p.204 ("Fill in: the number of children who like Mathematics...."). Pairs compare their counts; any mismatch is resolved by recounting together. Teacher notes the counts agreed on the board.

Students complete Now look at the above table and answer the following questions, p.205 ("Identify the most common and least common favourite subject...."). A short class discussion follows: which display — the raw list or the table — made it quicker to answer? Students record their reason in one sentence.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is miscounting the raw list by losing track of position; encourage students to cross off or dot each abbreviation as they count. T-3 (filling the formal frequency table) is set as homework so students practise transferring their verified counts independently — it can also be used as additional in-class practice if time allows.

section_titles: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
periods.activity_title: Count the icons, read the picture

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Look at the information given above, p.206
tasks_in_class.description: Colour the outline drawings of golas to match the colours shown in Rohan's and Anjali's data records.
Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least? How do you know?
Which of the ways of representing data did you use to answer these questions and why?

time_bands.activity: Students look at both pictographs (Rohan's figure icons and Anjali's lolly icons) on pp.206–207 without reading questions. Teacher asks: 'What do you notice? What does each icon stand for? How are the two charts different?' Students share observations.

Students complete Look at the information given above, p.206 ("Colour the outline drawings of golas to match the colours...."). Students colour carefully, then count icons for each colour in both representations to build a mental picture of the quantities.

Students answer Q1, p.206 ("Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least?....). They write their reasoning: which chart did they count from, and why? Teacher prompts: 'Is it easier to count the figures or the lolly icons for this question?'
Students answer Q5, p.207 ("Which of the ways of representing data did you use...."). A brief share-out closes the unit: students state which representation helped and why.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes count the same icon twice when the rows are long; suggest they use a finger or pencil tip to move along each row systematically. Additional questions Q2–Q4 (pp.206–207) can be used as further practice — Q2 asks which colour Anjali and Rohan would choose, Q3 asks which colour boys ate most, and Q4 asks which colour girls ate most.

section_titles: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
periods.activity_title: Boys, girls, and their gola choices

tasks_in_class.description: Which colour gola would Anjali and Rohan have bought?
Which colour golas did boys eat the most?
Which colour golas did girls eat the most?

time_bands.activity: Students re-examine the two gola pictographs on pp.206–207. Teacher asks two warm-up questions orally: 'Which representation separates boys and girls?' and 'Which representation mixes them together?' Students identify which chart is which and explain.

Students answer Q2, p.206 ("Which colour gola would Anjali and Rohan have bought?") and Q3, p.207 ("Which colour golas did boys eat the most?"). They record which chart they used for each question and why that chart was better suited.

Students answer Q4, p.207 ("Which colour golas did girls eat the most?"). Pairs compare: did you use the same chart as for Q3 or a different one? Why? Students articulate in writing the difference between a chart that separates groups and one that shows totals.
Class discussion: when is it useful to show boys and girls separately versus together? Students connect this to the idea that a data representation should be chosen to match the question being asked.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently assume both pictographs show the same information in the same way; the key insight is that Rohan's representation separates boys from girls while Anjali's combines them — making each chart better suited to different questions. Watch for students who answer Q3 and Q4 using the combined chart; ask them to check using the chart that separates by group.

section_titles: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
periods.activity_title: Survey the class, build a two-way table

tasks_in_class.description: Find out from your classmates how many of them play only chess, only cricket, both or neither. Record in the space provided.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Now let us organise the above data in the table, p.207
tasks_in_class.description: Fill the two-way table: rows Chess only / Cricket only / Both / Neither; columns No. of Girls and No. of Boys.

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the four categories by writing them on the board: Chess only / Cricket only / Both / Neither. Each student decides which category applies to them. Teacher asks: 'Why do we need four categories? Could one student belong to two categories?' Students discuss.

Students circulate and complete Activity — Chess or Cricket, p.207 ("Find out from your classmates how many of them play only chess, only cricket, both or neither...."). They use a simple tally, keeping boys and girls separate as they record.

Students return to their seats and complete Now let us organise the above data in the table, p.207 ("Fill the two-way table: rows Chess only / Cricket only / Both / Neither; columns No. of Girls and No. of Boys...."). Teacher circulates and asks: 'Does the total of girls + boys in each row match your tally?' Students verify row by row.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes place 'Both' children into each single-game row as well, double-counting them — clarify that the four categories are mutually exclusive and together cover everyone. Checking that all row totals add to the class size is a useful self-verification habit to build.

section_titles: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
periods.activity_title: Interpret the table, then meet the Bal Mela pictograph

tasks_in_class.description: Answer: (1) Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls? (2) Who plays Cricket the most — Boys or Girls? (3) How many children play both types of games?
Complete the table: total sold items for Fruit Chaats and Sandwiches across all three days.

time_bands.activity: Students open to the two-way table they completed in the previous unit on chess and cricket. They answer Answer these questions, p.207 ("Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls?...."). Teacher asks: 'Which column did you look at? How does the table make comparison quicker than a raw list?'

Students turn to p.208 and examine the two Bal Mela pictographs — one for fruit chaats and one for sandwiches. Teacher asks: 'What does each icon stand for? How many items does one icon represent?' Students identify the key before counting.

Students complete Let Us Do Q1, p.208 ("Complete the table: total sold items for Fruit Chaats and Sandwiches across all three days...."). They count icons for each row and record totals, then check that the numbers look reasonable by comparing row sizes visually.

periods.teacher_notes: When reading the Bal Mela pictograph, students sometimes forget to multiply by the icon value (the key) and simply count icons as single units — prompt them to check the key before writing any number. Comparing two-way table interpretation with pictograph interpretation helps students see that both tools organise the same kind of comparison question.

section_titles: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
periods.activity_title: Which day sold the most? Totals and comparisons

tasks_in_class.description: On which day were the most sandwiches sold?
Which item had the highest sale on Day 2?
Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales.

time_bands.activity: Students revisit the Bal Mela pictograph on p.208. Teacher poses orally: 'Without computing, which day do you think had the most sandwiches? How are you guessing?' Students estimate by comparing icon rows visually, then verify by counting.

Students answer Let Us Do Q2, p.208 ("On which day were the most sandwiches sold?") and Let Us Do Q3, p.208 ("Which item had the highest sale on Day 2?"). They record which row or column they read and state the comparison they made.

Students complete Let Us Do Q4, p.208 ("Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales...."). They add fruit chaat and sandwich totals for each day, circle the highest, and explain in one sentence how they identified it.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes add across all three days for a single item instead of adding both items for a single day — clarify that Q4 asks for the combined total per day, not the grand total per item. Having students name exactly which numbers they are adding before they write the sum helps catch this error.

periods.activity_title: Design, collect, display and compare — the full data journey

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses a fresh survey question to the class: 'Which fruit do you like best — mango, banana, apple or orange?' Students recognise this as the kind of well-framed question studied in the framing a question and collecting data section — one choice per person, comparable answers. Each student writes their choice on a slip.

Teacher collects slips and reads them aloud; students tally responses using stroke marks, then transfer counts into a frequency table drawn on the board — rows: fruit names; column: number of children. The class identifies the most and least liked fruit from the table, connecting this to the organising data into a frequency table work done earlier.

Small groups each design a simple pictograph of the same fruit data on paper — choosing an icon and deciding how many items each icon represents. Groups post their pictographs. The class reads one group's pictograph: count the icons, apply the key, verify the total matches the table. This connects the pictograph reading practised in the Colourful Golas and Bal Mela sections.

Teacher introduces a two-variable question: 'Does your choice differ by row?' Students quickly raise hands by row and the class builds a two-row version of the table (one row per classroom row), echoing the two-way table structure from the Chess or Cricket section. A final discussion: 'Which display answered each question most easily?' consolidates the chapter's central idea that the choice of display depends on the question being asked.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together framing a survey question, tallying into a frequency table, constructing and reading a pictograph, and using a two-way structure — if students struggle at the pictograph step, return to the idea that the key (one icon = a fixed number) must be applied before any comparison is valid. Watch for students who draw icons without agreeing on a key first.

items.section_title: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
items.prompt: On p.206 there is a row of gola outline drawings. There are 2 orange golas, 4 green golas, and 1 red gola. Colour each drawing with the correct colour to match this information. Then write the name of the colour that appears the most.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 drawings coloured orange, 4 coloured green, 1 coloured red. The colour that appears the most is green.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count how many of each colour are listed, colour accordingly, then compare the counts to find the largest.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student colour one at a time using the count; stretch: ask them to make a new row where blue appears the most.

exercise.book_ref: Look at the information given above, p.206
exercise.description: Colour the outline drawings of golas to match the colours shown in Rohan's and Anjali's data records.

items.section_title: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
items.prompt: A student says she plays chess and cricket. Which category should she be placed in when filling a two-way table like the Chess or Cricket table?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether the student plays chess, cricket, both, or neither — she plays both, so she belongs in the 'Both' row.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student focuses only on chess and ignores that cricket is also mentioned — partial reading of the information.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student focuses only on cricket and ignores that chess is also mentioned — partial reading of the information.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has misread the question or confused 'neither' with 'both games' — a reversal error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student point to each game the child plays and check the four category descriptions one by one; stretch: ask what category a child who plays only volleyball would belong to.

exercise.description: Find out from your classmates how many of them play only chess, only cricket, both or neither. Record in the space provided.

items.section_title: Framing a question and collecting data
items.prompt: Priya wants to find out which sport is most popular in her class. She thinks of two questions to ask: Question 1 — 'Do you like any sports?' and Question 2 — 'Which one sport do you like the most?' Which question should Priya use, and why?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya should use Question 2. Question 2 asks for exactly one choice, so every answer can be counted and compared fairly. Question 1 gives a yes/no answer that does not tell which sport is most popular.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether each question produces a single, comparable answer that can be counted — only Question 2 does.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student what kind of answer each question produces and whether those answers can be placed in a table; stretch: ask the student to write a third question that would be even clearer.

exercise.book_ref: Look at the questions asked by Rohan and Anjali, p.203
exercise.description: Tick the question that is the most appropriate for finding the 'most liked subject'. Why do you think so? Discuss with your friends and teacher.

items.section_title: Organising data into a frequency table
items.prompt: A class of 30 children was asked to choose one favourite colour. The frequency table shows: Red — 12, Blue — 8, Green — 6, Yellow — 4. Which statement is correct?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Colour | Number of children |
| Red | 12 |
| Blue | 8 |
| Green | 6 |
| Yellow | 4 |

options.label: A
options.text: Blue is the most liked colour.

options.label: B
options.text: Green and Blue together are liked by more children than Red.

options.label: C
options.text: Red is the most liked and Yellow is the least liked colour.

options.label: D
options.text: Yellow is the most liked colour.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Red is the most liked colour (12 children) and Yellow is the least liked (4 children).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the largest number in the frequency column for most liked, and the smallest for least liked.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the smallest frequency with the largest — a reading reversal error.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Green (6) + Blue (8) = 14, which is greater than Red (12), so this statement is actually true — however this option tests whether the student checks both parts of option C correctly; a student choosing B may not have looked at Red's total carefully.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has picked the second-largest value instead of the largest — a near-miss comparison error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student underline the largest and smallest numbers in the table before answering; stretch: ask which two colours together equal exactly the number who like Red.

exercise.description: Identify the most common and least common favourite subject. Then decide which of the two ways of displaying information (raw list vs. table) is easier to understand and why.

items.section_title: Reading and interpreting a pictograph (Colourful Golas)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows golas eaten by children. The pink row has 5 lolly icons and the orange row has 3 lolly icons. Each icon stands for 2 golas. Which colour was eaten the most, and how many golas of that colour were eaten?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Pink was eaten the most. Pink: 5 icons × 2 = 10 golas. Orange: 3 icons × 2 = 6 golas. So pink golas (10) were eaten more than orange golas (6).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the icons in each row, multiply by the key value (2), then compare the results.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write out the multiplication for each row step by step before comparing; stretch: ask how many more pink golas were eaten than orange golas.

exercise.description: Which colour ice gola do the children eat (a) the most and (b) the least? How do you know?

items.section_title: Collecting and organising data in a two-way table (Chess or Cricket)
items.prompt: Look at the two-way table below. Who plays Cricket the most — boys or girls?
items.visual_stimulus:
| Nature of Game | No. of Girls | No. of Boys |
| Chess only | 5 | 3 |
| Cricket only | 4 | 9 |
| Both | 2 | 2 |
| Neither | 1 | 3 |

options.label: A
options.text: Boys, because 9 boys play Cricket only and that is more than 4 girls.

options.label: B
options.text: Boys, because boys play more Chess.

options.label: C
options.text: Girls, because 5 girls play Chess only.

options.label: D
options.text: Girls, because they have more students overall.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Boys play Cricket the most. The Cricket only row shows 9 boys compared to 4 girls, so boys have the higher count.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the 'Cricket only' row and compare the number in the Girls column with the number in the Boys column.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is comparing overall totals rather than reading the specific Cricket only row — a row-selection error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has read the Chess only row instead of the Cricket only row — a row confusion error.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reached the correct group (boys) but cited the wrong row (Chess) as the reason — reasoning based on wrong evidence.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to place a finger on the Cricket only row and then read across to Girls and Boys before comparing; stretch: ask the student to find out how many children play cricket in total (Cricket only + Both) for boys and girls.

exercise.description: Answer: (1) Who plays Chess the most — Boys or Girls? (2) Who plays Cricket the most — Boys or Girls? (3) How many children play both types of games?

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows sandwich sales over three days. Each sandwich icon stands for 10 sandwiches. Day 1 has 3 icons, Day 2 has 5 icons, and Day 3 has 4 icons. On which day were the most sandwiches sold?

options.label: B
options.text: Day 1 and Day 3 had the same sales.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Day 2 had the most sandwiches sold: 5 icons × 10 = 50 sandwiches. Day 1: 30, Day 3: 40.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the icons for each day, multiply by 10 (the key), then identify the largest total.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may have read only the first row without comparing all three — a premature stopping error.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has confused the second-largest with the largest, or miscounted Day 2's icons — a comparison error.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has incorrectly equated Day 1 (3 icons, 30 sandwiches) and Day 3 (4 icons, 40 sandwiches) — a miscounting or misreading error.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student write out the multiplication for each day before comparing; stretch: ask how many more sandwiches were sold on Day 2 than on Day 1.

exercise.description: On which day were the most sandwiches sold?

items.section_title: Organising data into a frequency table
items.prompt: A teacher collected 20 students' favourite colours: R R B G R B B R G R B G R R B G R B G R. How many students chose Blue (B)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 students chose Blue. Counting the B entries in the list: positions 6, 7, 11, 15, 18, 20 — total 6.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Go through the list from left to right and make a tally mark each time B appears, then count the tally marks.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student undercounted by 1 — likely missed one B in the middle of the list.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student overcounted by 1 — likely counted one letter that is not B, or marked a position twice.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student undercounted significantly — likely lost track of position and stopped early.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student cross out each letter as it is counted so no position is skipped; stretch: ask the student to fill in counts for all three colours and check that they add to 20.

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: A pictograph shows food sold at a fair. Each icon stands for 5 items. Fruit chaat: Day 1 — 4 icons, Day 2 — 3 icons, Day 3 — 6 icons. Sandwiches: Day 1 — 2 icons, Day 2 — 5 icons, Day 3 — 3 icons. What is the total number of fruit chaats sold across all three days?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total fruit chaats = (4 + 3 + 6) icons × 5 = 13 × 5 = 65 fruit chaats.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add the fruit chaat icons across all three days, then multiply the total by 5 (the key).
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student first add only the icons (4+3+6=13) and then multiply by 5 as a separate step; stretch: ask the student to also find the total sandwiches and compare which item sold more overall.

exercise.description: Complete the table: total sold items for Fruit Chaats and Sandwiches across all three days.

items.section_title: Reading a pictograph and computing totals (Bal Mela)
items.prompt: Using the same fair pictograph: each icon stands for 5 items. Fruit chaat icons — Day 1: 4, Day 2: 3, Day 3: 6. Sandwich icons — Day 1: 2, Day 2: 5, Day 3: 3. Find the combined total of both items sold on Day 2.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Day 2 fruit chaats: 3 × 5 = 15. Day 2 sandwiches: 5 × 5 = 25. Combined total on Day 2: 15 + 25 = 40 items.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each item's Day 2 icons by 5 to get item totals, then add the two item totals together.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student compute each item's Day 2 total separately before adding; stretch: ask the student to find which day had the highest combined total and by how much it exceeded Day 2.

exercise.description: Complete the total sales table (Day 1, Day 2, Day 3 combined) and circle the day that had the highest sales.
